subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A potential drawback of globalisation for a developed economy is:
options: greater access to global capital
wider consumer choice
lower prices for imported consumer goods
structural unemployment as production shifts to lower-cost economies
questions.explain: Globalisation can cause structural unemployment in higher-cost economies as labour-intensive production relocates abroad.

questions.q: Which policy is an expenditure-reducing measure to correct a current-account deficit?
options: Depreciation of the currency
Imposing import tariffs
Deflationary fiscal policy that lowers aggregate demand
Supply-side reforms to improve competitiveness
questions.explain: Expenditure-reducing policies cut domestic demand (e.g. tighter fiscal/monetary policy) to reduce import spending.

questions.q: Other things equal, a rise in a country's terms of trade means that:
options: the current account automatically moves into surplus
a given volume of exports buys a larger volume of imports
the exchange rate has necessarily depreciated
the country must export more to afford the same imports
questions.explain: An improvement in the terms of trade means export prices have risen relative to import prices, so each unit of exports commands more imports.

questions.q: Which of the following is most likely to cause a deterioration in a developing primary-exporter's terms of trade over the long run?
options: A persistent rise in world commodity prices
Low income elasticity of demand for primary products relative to manufactures
An appreciation of its currency
Membership of a customs union
questions.explain: The Prebisch-Singer hypothesis links low income elasticity for primaries (and high elasticity for manufactures) to a secular decline in primary exporters' terms of trade.

questions.q: Trade diversion occurs when the formation of a trading bloc causes a country to switch its imports from a:
options: monopolist to a competitive supplier
lower-cost external producer to a higher-cost member producer
higher-cost member to a lower-cost external producer
domestic firm to a foreign firm
questions.explain: Trade diversion is the welfare-reducing shift away from an efficient non-member toward a less efficient member because the latter avoids the external tariff.

questions.q: A 'managed float' (dirty float) exchange-rate system is one in which:
options: the rate floats but the central bank intervenes occasionally to influence it
exchange rates are abolished
the rate is permanently fixed to gold
the currency is pegged to a single foreign currency by law
questions.explain: Under a managed float the market broadly sets the rate but authorities intervene from time to time to smooth or steer movements.

questions.q: The primary remit of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is to:
options: set tariffs for member states
promote global monetary cooperation and provide short-term balance-of-payments support
finance long-term infrastructure projects
provide concessional loans only to the poorest countries
questions.explain: The IMF oversees the monetary system and lends to members facing balance-of-payments problems, often with conditionality.

questions.q: A principal role of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) is to:
options: oversee multilateral trade agreements and adjudicate trade disputes
provide development loans to low-income countries
set the value of members' exchange rates
fix world commodity prices
questions.explain: The WTO administers trade rules, promotes liberalisation and resolves disputes between members; lending and exchange rates fall to other bodies.

questions.q: Which is most clearly a barrier to economic development in many low-income countries?
options: A savings gap reflected in low investment and reliance on primary exports
Strong, well-enforced property rights
High rates of domestic saving and investment
Diversified, high-value manufacturing exports
questions.explain: A savings gap (low saving and investment), often alongside primary-product dependence, constrains capital accumulation and development.

questions.q: In the UK balance of payments, the current account does NOT include the:
options: primary income (investment income) balance
trade in goods balance
trade in services balance
purchase of foreign equities by UK residents
questions.explain: Purchases of foreign equities are financial-account transactions; the current account covers trade, primary income and secondary income.

questions.q: Globalisation has been driven by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: falling transport and communication costs
rising worldwide tariff barriers
containerisation and improved logistics
trade liberalisation and the growth of multinationals
questions.explain: Globalisation has been propelled by falling barriers, cheaper transport/communication and MNCs; rising tariffs work against it.

questions.q: The terms of trade for a country are best defined as the:
options: tariff revenue collected on imported goods
volume of exports divided by the volume of imports
value of the current account as a share of GDP
index of export prices divided by the index of import prices, times 100
questions.explain: The terms of trade = (index of average export prices / index of average import prices) x 100.

questions.q: The Harrod-Domar model emphasises that economic growth depends primarily on the:
options: level of the exchange rate
size of the tariff barrier
savings ratio and the capital-output ratio
number of trading blocs joined
questions.explain: Harrod-Domar links the growth rate to the savings ratio divided by the capital-output ratio, stressing investment.

questions.q: Under a freely floating exchange-rate system, the external value of a currency is determined by:
options: the supply of and demand for the currency on the foreign-exchange market
the rate set by the IMF
the central bank's official target
the level of foreign-exchange reserves held
questions.explain: In a clean float the rate is set purely by market supply and demand, with no official intervention.

questions.q: A quota differs from a tariff on the same import in that a quota:
options: reduces the domestic price of the good
always generates revenue for the government
is permitted without restriction under WTO rules
caps the physical quantity of imports rather than taxing them
questions.explain: A quota is a quantitative limit on imports; unlike a tariff it does not automatically raise revenue and the scarcity rent may accrue to importers.

questions.q: To maintain a fixed exchange rate above its market equilibrium, a central bank would need to:
options: buy its own currency using foreign-exchange reserves
sell its own currency and buy foreign reserves
stop all foreign trade
lower interest rates sharply
questions.explain: Defending an overvalued peg requires buying domestic currency (selling reserves) to offset excess supply.

questions.q: A country has a comparative advantage in producing a good when it can produce that good at a lower:
options: level of total factor productivity
absolute quantity than its trading partner
opportunity cost than its trading partner
monetary price using domestic currency
questions.explain: Comparative advantage rests on the lower opportunity cost of production, not on absolute output or price.

questions.q: The deadweight welfare loss from a tariff arises because:
options: government revenue exceeds the cost of administration
domestic firms earn higher profits
resources are misallocated through inefficient domestic production and reduced consumption
foreign exporters absorb the full tariff
questions.explain: Tariffs create deadweight loss via the production-distortion (inefficient home output) and consumption-distortion (reduced consumption) triangles.

questions.q: A criticism of relying on foreign aid as a development strategy is that it may:
options: guarantee export-led growth
always remove the savings gap permanently
create dependency and weaken incentives for domestic reform
raise the recipient's terms of trade automatically
questions.explain: Aid can foster dependency, distort incentives and be lost to corruption, which is why some economists favour trade over aid.

questions.q: Export-led growth as a development strategy typically relies on:
options: reducing the savings ratio
exploiting comparative advantage to expand output sold abroad
raising import tariffs to protect all home industries
fixing prices below market levels
questions.explain: Export-led (outward-looking) growth uses trade and comparative advantage to widen markets and raise productivity.

questions.q: A customs union differs from a free-trade area because members of a customs union also:
options: harmonise all fiscal policy
allow free movement of labour and capital
operate a common external tariff against non-members
adopt a single common currency
questions.explain: A customs union combines internal free trade with a common external tariff, distinguishing it from a simple free-trade area.

questions.q: The Marshall-Lerner condition states that a currency depreciation will improve the trade balance only if the:
options: income elasticity of imports is less than one
sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceeds one
capital account is in surplus
exchange rate is fixed by the central bank
questions.explain: Marshall-Lerner: depreciation improves the current account when the combined (absolute) price elasticities of export and import demand are greater than unity.

questions.q: A current-account deficit on the balance of payments means that, broadly:
options: the government budget is in deficit
exports of goods and services exceed imports
imports of goods and services (plus net income/transfers) exceed exports
the financial account is in deficit
questions.explain: A current-account deficit arises when outflows for imports, income and transfers exceed the corresponding inflows from exports.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-tariff barrier to trade?
options: A floating exchange rate
Strict domestic technical and safety standards applied to imports
A specific per-unit tax on imports
An ad valorem import duty
questions.explain: Non-tariff barriers include regulations, standards and administrative rules that restrict imports without using a formal tariff.

questions.q: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines life expectancy, education and:
options: the Gini coefficient
gross national income per capita (PPP)
the current-account balance
the unemployment rate
questions.explain: HDI is a composite of life expectancy at birth, mean/expected years of schooling and GNI per head at PPP.

questions.q: Country X can produce both wheat and cloth using fewer resources than Country Y. According to comparative advantage, mutually beneficial trade is still possible provided:
options: both countries fix their exchange rates
Country X has a balance-of-payments surplus
the opportunity-cost ratios of the two goods differ between the countries
Country Y subsidises its exports
questions.explain: Gains from trade arise whenever opportunity-cost (and hence relative-cost) ratios differ, even if one country has absolute advantage in both goods.

questions.q: A depreciation of the pound against the dollar will, other things equal:
options: leave the prices of traded goods unchanged
make UK exports dearer and imports cheaper in foreign-currency terms
always reduce the UK current-account deficit immediately
make UK exports cheaper to foreigners and imports dearer for UK buyers
questions.explain: Depreciation lowers the foreign-currency price of exports and raises the domestic price of imports (WPIDEC / SPICED).

questions.q: A tariff imposed by a small importing country on a good will most directly cause:
options: an increase in domestic consumer surplus
a reduction in government revenue
a rise in domestic production and a fall in imports
a fall in the domestic price of the good
questions.explain: A tariff raises the domestic price, encouraging domestic supply and reducing imports while generating tariff revenue.

questions.q: The J-curve effect describes how, following a currency depreciation, the trade balance:
options: moves only if the exchange rate is fixed
improves immediately and then worsens
worsens at first before improving as quantities adjust
remains constant throughout
questions.explain: In the short run demand is inelastic so the trade balance worsens; as volumes respond over time it improves, tracing a J shape.

questions.q: A key limitation of using GDP per capita alone to measure development is that it:
options: always overstates inflation
ignores distribution, non-marketed output and quality-of-life factors
excludes government spending
cannot be measured at purchasing-power parity
questions.explain: GDP per head says nothing about income distribution, informal activity, health, education or environmental quality.
